comments.body:
Thanks for checking the implementation and test coverage.

My expectation as the reporter is that `method="auto"` would select the method independently for each slice, so that batching the same inputs preserves the results of separate calls. A slice’s own data would then determine which method is used.

Whether this matches the intended API behavior is what I was hoping the maintainers could clarify. If selecting one method for the entire call is intentional, explicitly documenting that another slice’s ties can change the selected method and p-value would help. If per-slice selection is intended, the mixed tied/untied example above could serve as a regression test.
comments.author: tasuku-kobayashi

comments.body:
I looked a little further at the current implementation and existing test coverage.

`test_gh_12837_11113` already establishes that, for explicit `method="exact"` and `method="asymptotic"`, a batched call should produce the same per-slice results as calling each pair separately. The mixed-tie `method="auto"` case appears to be the exception because the tie check is reduced globally:

```python
xp.any(t > 1)
```

I think a per-slice `auto` implementation could be fairly bounded:

* keep the current behavior when both sample sizes are greater than 8 (`asymptotic`);
* otherwise determine the tie condition along the sample axis, e.g. `xp.any(t > 1, axis=-1)`;
* use the existing vectorized exact and asymptotic calculations and select the p-value per slice according to that mask.

This would leave 1-D behavior unchanged, leave explicit `method="exact"` and `method="asymptotic"` unchanged, and only change multidimensional `method="auto"` calls in which some slices contain ties and others do not.

For small samples, computing both candidate p-values and selecting between them may also be a relatively simple implementation option, since the exact path is already vectorized for batched input. I have not attempted to choose the preferred implementation strategy here.

A dedicated regression test should use an explicit mixture of tied and untied slices. Simply adding `"auto"` to `test_gh_12837_11113` would probably not exercise the problem because its random input normally has no ties.

If global method selection is intentional instead, I think the documentation would need to make the scope explicit: “there are no ties” currently reads naturally as a property of each sample pair, whereas the implementation means no ties anywhere in the broadcasted call.

So my preference remains per-slice selection, principally because it preserves the existing batched-versus-separate equivalence for each unchanged sample pair.

issues.body:

Dear Scipy Team,

I would like to report a potential issue with the implementation of Dice Coefficient in Scipy.

According to [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%B8rensen%E2%80%93Dice_coefficient) (see section "Difference from Jaccard") and papers such as [this](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4533825/) (see Equations (8) and (9)), there is a direct relationship between the Dice Coefficient and the Jaccard Index. 

However, when I calculated the Dice Coefficient using the Scipy package and compared with the results obtained by using this direct relationship with the Jaccard Index, the results doesn't match. I have also calculated Dice using the metrics from the Confusion Matrix (eg. TP, FP etc.), and the results doesn't match with the Scipy package.

I have included an example showing this here: https://github.com/leockl/Dice-Coefficient/blob/master/Dice.ipynb

Could someone have a look at this. Many thanks.


#### Scipy/Numpy/Python version information:
1.4.1 1.18.1 sys.version_info(major=3, minor=7, micro=6, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
issues.author: leockl

comments.body:
The functions in `scipy.spatial.distance` compute *distances* or *dissimilarities*.  The references that you gave are using the *similiarity* indices.  For `dice` and `jaccard`, you can convert from one to the other with `similarity = 1 - dissimilarity`.

For example.

```
In [52]: y_true = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0]                                               

In [53]: y_pred = [1, 1, 0, 1, 1]                                               
```
Compute the Jaccard and Dice *dissimilarities*, and convert to the corresponding similarities:
```
In [55]: JAC_dis = distance.jaccard(y_true, y_pred) 

In [56]: JAC_sim = 1 - JAC_dis

In [57]: DICE_dis = distance.dice(y_true, y_pred)

In [58]: DICE_sim = 1 - DICE_dis
```
Verify that for the similarities, `DICE = 2*JAC / (JAC + 1)`:
                      
```
In [59]: DICE_sim                                                               
Out[59]: 0.5714285714285714

In [60]: 2*JAC_sim/(JAC_sim + 1)                                                
Out[60]: 0.5714285714285715
```

If not, happy for you to close this issue. 

Many thanks again.

`scipy.special.legendre` appears to give incorrect result for degrees higher than 3. Basic rules are:

```
       4             3        2
4.375 x + 4.857e-16 x - 3.75 x + 2.429e-16 x + 0.375
       5        3             2
7.875 x - 8.75 x - 4.372e-16 x + 1.875 x
```

comments.body:
This looks like the result of floating point imprecision in the method that is used to generate the coefficients.  Other polynomial functions have the same issue.  For example:
```
In [27]: from scipy.special import chebyt, chebyu, hermite

In [28]: chebyt(4)
Out[28]: 
poly1d([ 8.00000000e+00,  0.00000000e+00, -8.00000000e+00, -2.22044605e-16,
        1.00000000e+00])

In [29]: chebyu(4)
Out[29]: 
poly1d([ 1.6000000e+01,  0.0000000e+00, -1.2000000e+01, -4.4408921e-16,
        1.0000000e+00])

In [30]: hermite(4)
Out[30]: 
poly1d([ 1.6000000e+01,  0.0000000e+00, -4.8000000e+01, -8.8817842e-16,
        1.2000000e+01])
```

The functions are defined in [`orthogonal.py`](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/master/scipy/special/orthogonal.py), and it looks like it would be a simple change to zero out the coefficients that we know should be zero in functions such as `legendre`, `chebyt`, `chebyu`, and `hermite`.   Does anyone see a reason to not do this?
comments.author: WarrenWeckesser

comments.body:
I think it would be pointless, roundoff error would still bite once the polynomial was evaluated. The precision can probably be improved by using a more careful algorithm, but not significantly.
```
In [12]: H.basis(4).convert(kind=P).coef                                                                                                
Out[12]: array([ 12.,   0., -48.,   0.,  16.])
```
Note the reversal of coefficient order. It's prettier, but that may mostly be the printing precision. If you really want exactness, symbolic math over the rationals is the way to go, but that is a different package.

issues.title: BUG: scipy.stats.f_oneway(equal_var=False) numerical instability and overflow on extremely small input scales
issues.body:
### Describe your issue.

When running Welch's ANOVA via `scipy.stats.f_oneway(..., equal_var=False)`, scale invariance breaks down under extremely small input scales (e.g., scaled down by $2^{-511}$). The function emits overflow warnings and yields an incorrect F-statistic and p-value, changing the statistical significance outcome at $\alpha = 0.05$.

### Expected behavior

Welch's ANOVA is mathematically scale-invariant. For the example below, scaling all inputs uniformly should yield:

- **F-statistic:** $72 / 7 \approx 10.285714$
- **Degrees of freedom:** $(2, 4)$
- **p-value:** $49 / 1849 \approx 0.02650081125$

### Actual behavior

For the scaled input:

- **F-statistic:** $\approx 21.81818$
- **p-value:** $\approx 0.05611184474$ (decision flips at $\alpha = 0.05$)
- **Warnings:** overflow warnings, provided in the Error message field below.

### Cause analysis

The sample variances $s_i^2$ remain within the normal float64 range, and the individual Welch weights $w_i = n_i / s_i^2$ remain finite. However, summing these weights, $W = \sum_i w_i$, overflows, leading to incorrect values in subsequent calculations.

### Context / practical impact

This behavior was observed during boundary test validation using artificially scaled-down inputs ($2^{-511}$). While the occurrence frequency in typical practical data has not been formally assessed, numerical stability should ideally be preserved where floating-point representation permits.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Inputs
a = np.array([-1, 0, 1], dtype=np.float64)
b = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float64)
c = np.array([3, 4, 5], dtype=np.float64)

# Exact scaling factor without precision loss
scale = 2.0 ** (-511)

# Execution
res_orig = stats.f_oneway(a, b, c, equal_var=False)
res_scaled = stats.f_oneway(a * scale, b * scale, c * scale, equal_var=False)

print("Original:", res_orig)
print("Scaled:  ", res_scaled)
```

```shell

captured with warnings.simplefilter('always'):

RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in reduce

The saved log contains warning categories and messages only;
source filenames and line numbers were not recorded.
```

issues.title: `sigma=None` with `absolute_sigma=True` in `scipy.optimize.curve_fit()` unsenseful
issues.body:
Leaving `sigma=None` **and** putting `absolute_sigma=True` in `scipy.optimize.curve_fit()` still gives an output, which  potentially entails wrongly interpreted results because in this very case a) the weighting is defaulted to unity and b) the option `absolute_sigma=True` makes `scipy.optimize.curve_fit()` *think* the real errors are all ones. The correct output would be only given by `curve_fit(func, x_data, y_data)` with `absolute_sigma=False` which is the default already and the covariance matrix being scaled as already implemented.

Inserting the following query here https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/v1.5.1/scipy/optimize/minpack.py#L766 in `scipy.optimize.curve_fit()` would avoid a wrong unintend use:
```
    ...
    elif absolute_sigma:
        raise ValueError("sigma=None and absolute_sigma=True should not be used at the same time!")
    else:
        transform = None
```
        
and in the docstring:

```
        ...
        
    absolute_sigma : bool, optional
        If True, `sigma` is used in an absolute sense and the estimated parameter
        covariance `pcov` reflects these absolute values, i.e., `pcov` is not scaled by the reduced chi-squared.
        Can not be used together with `sigma=None`.

```

```
y = np.asfarray([1, 2.5, 3, 4])

def func(x, a, b):
    return a*x+b

with assert_raises(ValueError, match="sigma=None and absolute_sigma=True should not be used at the same time!"):
    curve_fit(func, x, y, absolute_sigma=True)
```

```
Failed: DID NOT RAISE <class 'ValueError'>
```

issues.title: ENH: consider a limited-memory regularized quasi-Newton method for scipy.optimize.minimize
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

# ENH: consider a limited-memory regularized quasi-Newton method for scipy.optimize.minimize

Hello, SciPy maintainers.
I'm Hiroki Hamaguchi, a doctoral student working in numerical optimization.

I greatly appreciate your work on SciPy, and I would like to discuss a possible addition to `scipy.optimize.minimize`.

(I previously mentioned this work in my presentation at [SciPyData 2026](https://scipydata.connpass.com/event/364718/) in Japan.)

This issue has two related motivations:

1. On some problems, the current L-BFGS-B implementation has a relatively large wall-clock cost per iteration.
2. Recent regularized quasi-Newton methods provide an alternative to the traditional line-search L-BFGS framework and may be faster or more robust on some problems.

I am therefore considering adding a new, Python-based, limited-memory regularized quasi-Newton method as an additional `minimize` method, but this plan is still tentative.

In this issue, I would like to ask whether this would be a reasonable direction for SciPy, and if so, whether you have any suggestions for the API or other design considerations.

## Motivations

### Per-iteration wall-clock cost

The first motivation is the current L-BFGS-B overhead.

SciPy's current implementation is written in [C](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/main/scipy/optimize/src/lbfgsb.c), exposed through Python by [`minimize(method="L-BFGS-B")`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/optimize.minimize-lbfgsb.html).

I would first like to clarify that this point is not directly related to the recent [SciPy issue #23191](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/23191), which reports a performance regression between SciPy 1.14 and releases from 1.15 onward and discusses OpenBLAS thread behavior as an important possible cause.

(I also have some interest in this issue, but I do not intend to discuss it further here.)

The key observation is that, on some problems, the current L-BFGS-B implementation has a relatively large wall-clock cost per iteration, regardless of the SciPy version or BLAS threading behavior.

The following figures are the benchmark results of the current L-BFGS-B implementation and our Python-based limited-memory quasi-Newton methods on two simple problems.
Please note that these results only illustrate the per-iteration wall-clock cost, which is independent of the theoretical efficiency of the optimization method.

As shown, our methods have lower per-iteration wall-clock costs at many of the tested dimensions. Our methods can be more than 2 times faster than the current L-BFGS-B implementation at some dimensions.
The main exceptions are small problems and dimensions near the BLAS threading crossover around $n=10^4$.

| Problem: Zero-chain quadratic | Problem: Diagonal quadratic |
| :---: | :---: |
| ![Zero-chain elapsed time versus dimension](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/SciPy/experiment1_zero_chain_dimension_scaling.png) | ![Diagonal-quadratic elapsed time versus dimension](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/SciPy/experiment2_diagonal_quadratic_dimension_scaling.png) |

A similar tendency appears with different L-BFGS memory values.

![Elapsed time for L-BFGS memory values 3 and 10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/SciPy/experiment3_lbfgs_memory_comparison.png)

Restricting all BLAS thread pools to one thread improves the relative performance of the Python methods, which outperform the current SciPy implementation at all but the smallest tested dimensions.

![Default and single-threaded BLAS comparison](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/SciPy/experiment4_blas_thread_comparison.png)

Further details are provided in [`notebooks/SciPy_issue.ipynb`](https://github.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/blob/main/notebooks/SciPy_issue.ipynb), a separate reproduction and diagnostic notebook.

I think that improving the C-based implementation in SciPy would be difficult, since I have already tried to reduce the overhead, but all of these attempts have failed.
This might be due to unavoidable Python--C transition overhead in the current implementation.

This is one of the motivations for proposing a new solver.

### Recent progress in quasi-Newton methods

The second motivation is recent progress in quasi-Newton methods.

The method I would like to propose in the future is the noise-tolerant regularized quasi-Newton method (NTRQN) described in our paper: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10642](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10642).

(I would like to make clear that this proposal is not intended as self-promotion. If the maintainers consider the method unsuitable, I will not pursue the proposal.)

Although the particular combination is ours, many of its components build on developments from the numerical optimization literature over the past several decades:

- **Regularized quasi-Newton directions:** these methods compute a direction corresponding to $-(B_k+\mu_k I)^{-1}g_k$, following regularized Newton and limited-memory RQN work ([Ueda and Yamashita, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10589-014-9656-x); [Kanzow and Steck, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12532-023-00238-4)). Compared with line-search L-BFGS, this approach can be more robust or faster on some problems.
- **Curvature safeguards independent of Wolfe success:** damped BFGS and cautious selection of stored pairs maintain usable, spectrally bounded limited-memory approximations. This follows the cautious-update tradition ([Li and Fukushima, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1052623499354242)).
- **Optional modified secant information:** when function values are reliable, information from function-value interpolation can improve the curvature model, following the modified-secant literature ([Zhang, Deng and Chen, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1021898630001); [Yabe, Ogasawara and Yoshino, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cam.2006.05.018)). Roughly speaking, this incorporates function-value interpolation, similar to that used in the Moré--Thuente line search in L-BFGS-B, into the quasi-Newton model update itself.
- **Use function values only when they are informative:** a relaxed, non-monotone Armijo test keeps ordinary quasi-Newton behavior when sufficient progress is observable. Otherwise, positive regularization is controlled by accumulated gradient norms, following the Objective-Function-Free Optimization (OFFO)/AdaGrad-Norm line of work ([Gratton, Jerad and Toint, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1080/10556788.2023.2296431), [Our paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10642)).

### Describe the solution you'd like.

## Benchmarking

Below are some benchmark results illustrating the performance of the proposed method.

[CUTEst](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10589-014-9687-3) is a standard collection and testing environment for optimization problems.
We conducted tests on 220 unconstrained problems at 64-bit precision and 124 at 32-bit precision.
The limited-memory methods used $m=10$, and the maximum iteration count was 15,000.

The primary figures use Dolan--Moré [performance profiles](https://doi.org/10.1007/s101070100263).
For problem $p$ and solver $s$, the ratio is $r_{p,s}=\frac{n_{p,s}}{\min_{s'} n_{p,s'}}$, where $n_{p,s}$ is the number of oracle calls (i.e., function and gradient evaluations) required to reach the stated gradient tolerance (and is infinite on failure).
At $\tau=1$, the height is the fraction of problems on which a solver was best.
At larger $\tau$, the height is the fraction solved within $\tau$ times the best solver's oracle count.
The final height therefore indicates robustness/coverage.

| 64-bit, $\|g\|_\infty\le10^{-5}$ | 32-bit, $\|g\|_\infty\le10^{-3}$ |
| :---: | :---: |
| ![64-bit performance profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/imgs/compare/_pp_precision64_gtol1e-05.png) | ![32-bit performance profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/imgs/compare/_pp_precision32_gtol1e-03.png) |

![Legend for performance profiles](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/main/doc/imgs/compare/_legend.png)

We note that these benchmark results only illustrate the number of oracle calls, not the wall-clock time (to maintain the reproducibility and fairness of the benchmark).
Combined with the low per-iteration wall-clock cost mentioned above, these results suggest that our method would be competitive in wall-clock time on many problems.

We plan to prepare a full set of wall-clock-time benchmark results before I formally submit a PR to SciPy.
Our paper is currently under review, and these results may be updated.


### Describe alternatives you've considered.

## Box constraints (the "-B" in L-BFGS-B)

The method can be extended to box constraints, which would be necessary for a full L-BFGS-B replacement.

A working prototype, [`qnlab/solver/qn_ntrqnb.py`](https://github.com/HirokiHamaguchi/qnlab/blob/main/qnlab/solver/qn_ntrqnb.py), combines our method with a generalized Cauchy point and is able to solve box-constrained problems.

However, I do not currently plan to include this box-constrained variant.
It would add substantial implementation and maintenance cost.
Box support could be considered later if there is sufficient user and maintainer interest.


### Additional context (e.g. screenshots, GIFs)

## Questions for SciPy maintainers

Thank you for reading this issue.
I would particularly appreciate feedback on the following points:

1. Do you think that a new, Python-based, limited-memory regularized quasi-Newton method is a reasonable addition to SciPy's `minimize`?
2. If so, do you have any suggestions for the API or other design considerations? (I recognize that adding a new method to `minimize` is a tough decision, e.g., [SciPy Issue #19918](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/19918), [SciPy PR #7729](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/7729))
3. (Optional) I am very interested in SciPy's development and would like to contribute to the project. Regarding the BLAS threading issue, I do not know whether the community already has plans to address it, but I would be glad to help with the investigation and/or implementation. If you have any suggestions, please let me know.

I will follow [SciPy's guidelines](https://scipy.org/contribute/) and will be responsive to maintainer feedback.
I am prepared to provide the implementation, tests, documentation, benchmarks, and follow-up maintenance.
Please let me know if you would like to see a prototype implementation or any additional information.

I would also like to mention @ilayn and @lorentzenchr with respect to their contributions to the L-BFGS-B method, as well as @AtsushiSakai, with whom I previously discussed this work at SciPyData 2026.

Thank you for considering the proposal.
issues.author: HirokiHamaguchi

comments.body:
Thank you @HirokiHamaguchi  this is a very nice demonstration. A few off-the-cuff remarks

 - The main issue with L-BFGS-B is that the code though I translated to C still uses Fortranisms because I did not want to introduce extra bugs. The linear algebra parts can use some makeup to increase performance. Especially the way how BFGS matrix is handled inline is suboptimal. 
 - The OpenBLAS issue is still in the back of our minds. But to eliminate this issue, I would suggest that you do the benchmarks with Conda environment linked to MKL library to get the true situation. 
 - reg. quasi-newton solvers are indeed very attractive but the phrase "for some problems" is a red flag for us because our pain points are always coming from the remaining problems. Bug reports typically don't come from good-weather branch but from the failure branches. Those are the typical shortcomings of academic solvers that they don't bother handling tons of edge cases that we have to watch out for. So if you cut any corners with "well that won't happen", they typically happen.
 - The python overhead is mostly coming from the python callback of the user function. Uniform `LowLevelCallback` support and relevant codegen is still something that we long for. 
 - The API can mimic the existing ones, there is also some interest in warm-starting so if the multipliers are available for warm starting that is also very important. 


> I am very interested in SciPy's development and would like to contribute to the project. Regarding the BLAS threading issue, I do not know whether the community already has plans to address it, but I would be glad to help with the investigation and/or implementation. If you have any suggestions, please let me know.

Any help is highly appreciated, we have a pretty flat hierarchy. As long as you communicate your intentions you are good to go. If you have some time to spare, profiling the optimization solver code would be highly appreciated. Then we would know where things are getting stuck (I suspect it is resetting BFGS array too often). If some BLAS calls are blocking then we can handroll some helper functions and avoid the bottlenecks. 

@andyfaff would also be interested in this.

comments.body:
@ilayn I profiled the solver as you suggested. The callback is not where the time goes.

Rosenbrock with analytic gradient, `jac=True`, 500 iterations, timing the objective from inside itself so the split is exact. Apple M1 Pro, scipy 1.18.1.

```
       n    m   wall_s     cb_s   cb_%   nit   nfev  us/iter outside cb
     100   10    0.023    0.006  25.2%   500    598              34.0
    1000   10    0.049    0.008  16.6%   500    593              82.2
   10000   10    0.355    0.026   7.4%   500    599             658.2
   10000   50    1.450    0.031   2.2%   500    593            2837.6
  100000   10    3.395    0.225   6.6%   500    596            6340.6
  100000   50   13.944    0.232   1.7%   500    600           27425.3
```

At n=1e5, m=50 the objective accounts for 1.7% of wall time. The callback share falls as n grows, so the cost is in `setulb`, not the Python boundary.

Cost is roughly linear in `maxcor`, as the two-loop recursion should be. The absolute level is the issue. Against a plain numpy two-loop recursion at the same m and n, no BLAS tuning, running at about 20 GB/s on this machine:

```
       n    m   scipy ms/iter   numpy two-loop ms   ratio
   10000   10           0.658               0.171    3.8
   10000   50           2.838               0.837    3.4
  100000   10           6.341               1.501    4.2
  100000   50          27.425               7.107    3.9
```

A consistent factor of about 4 above the dominant kernel, stable across both n and m.

Two caveats. The two-loop recursion is a lower bound on required work, not a model of L-BFGS-B: the Cauchy point and subspace minimisation are extra, and run here even with no bounds set. And this measures one machine and one problem family.

On your suspicion about resetting the BFGS array too often, I could not test it from Python. A counter on the skipped-update branch would settle it, and I am happy to build from source and instrument if you point me at the right branch.

If the factor of 4 holds up on your hardware, the flat per-iteration scaling in m suggests the arithmetic is right and the constant is not, which fits your remark about the inline matrix handling.

comments.body:
Thank you very much for the prompt and kind replies. I sincerely appreciate both the feedback.

For now, I would like to keep my response brief, but I will follow up with a more detailed reply, including profiling results, within about a week. I would be very grateful if you could give me a little time to investigate this properly.

## About NTQRN

Regarding @ilayn's concern about robustness and edge cases, I completely understand it, and I think it is a very important point. In fact, one of the original motivations behind NTRQN was precisely to address such difficult cases more carefully. For that reason, I believe this concern is actually something NTRQN may be particularly well positioned to address.

When I wrote that NTRQN performs well "for some problems," what I had in mind for the cases where NTRQN performs worse was something like this: a problem that takes 100 iterations with the current SciPy method might take 150 iterations with NTRQN. I did not mean that NTRQN works only on easy or favorable cases, or that its weakness lies in failing on difficult cases. In fact, one of the aspects we have focused on is precisely the opposite, i.e., reducing cases where an existing method fails to solve the problem at all, while NTRQN is still able to converge successfully.

For example, in the 32-bit, $\lVert g \rVert_\infty \leq 10^{-3}$ figure, the final solve rate of SciPy (red dashed line) is below 50%, whereas ours (blue) exceeds 70%. This difference is closely related to our efforts to handle precisely these kinds of difficult or edge cases.

Your comment also made me realize that it would probably be useful for this issue if I explained more concretely what kinds of cases cause the current SciPy solver to fail, and why NTRQN behaves differently in those cases.

Of course, if after looking into these details it turns out that the handling of corner cases is still not sufficiently robust, or that the practical benefit does not justify the additional maintenance burden for SciPy, I do not intend to push the proposal unnecessarily. This is something I am also personally quite concerned about. If this direction is of interest, I would be very happy to discuss these points in more detail in my follow-up.

## About Profiling

I will also run the benchmarks in an MKL-linked environment as suggested. And thank you very much, @MohammadSadeghSalehi, for the profiling results. I have not yet examine them carefully, but I will do so and respond to them properly in my follow-up.

Since the discussion about the new solver and the performance investigation of the existing L-BFGS-B implementation may become somewhat intertwined, I may open a separate issue for the latter if that seems cleaner.

---

Thank you again for the thoughtful and constructive responses. I really appreciate it, and I look forward to continuing the discussion.

I came across https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/17813 which suggests calculating Mahalanobis distance as:
d = xT.VI.x + yT.VI.y - xT.VI.y - yT.VI.x
instead of
d = (x-y)T.VI.(x-y)
so I wrote a quick test to compare cdist with their suggestion and another implementation of Mahalanobis distance.

```python
from time import time

from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
import numpy as np


SIZE=500
FEATURES=500
x = np.random.normal(size=(FEATURES,SIZE))
y = np.random.normal(size=(FEATURES,SIZE))
vi = np.linalg.inv(np.cov(np.vstack([x.T,y.T]).T)).T

start0 = time()
pwd_scipy = cdist(x.T,y.T,metric='mahalanobis',VI=vi)
fin0 = time() - start0

# calculate (x-y)T.VI.(x-y)
start1 = time()
for i in range(0,SIZE):
    yi =  y[:,i]
    e = (x.T - yi.T).T
    di = np.einsum('ij,ji->i',np.dot(e.T,vi),e)
    assert np.all(np.isclose(pwd_scipy[:,i],np.sqrt(di)))
fin1 = time() - start1


# calculate xT.VI.x + yT.VI.y - xT.VI.y - yT.VI.y
start2 = time()
xtvi = np.dot(x.T,vi)
xtvix = np.einsum('ij,ji->i',xtvi,x)
vix = np.dot(vi,x)
for i in range(0,SIZE):
    yi =  y[:,i]
    ytvi = np.dot(yi.T,vi)
    ytviy = np.dot(ytvi,yi)
    ytvix = np.dot(yi.T,vix)
    xtviy = np.dot(xtvi,yi)
    di = xtvix + ytviy - ytvix - xtviy
    assert np.all(np.isclose(pwd_scipy[:,i],np.sqrt(di)))
fin2 = time() - start2

print('scipy: {}'.format(fin0))
print('Std: {}'.format(fin1))
print('New: {}'.format(fin2))
```

comments.body:
In general, rearranging distance calculations like can cause accuracy issues. Especially in cases where `x` and `y` are large, but differ on a small scale. For example,
```python
>>> x = 1e12 * np.random.rand(100)
>>> y = x + np.random.rand(100)
>>> ((x-y)**2).sum()
37.50577463819013

>>> (x**2 - 2*x*y + y**2).sum()
-207583232.0
```

Not only is the distance wildly incorrect, it's also negative which should be impossible. So, I'm not sure this is appropriate for a general-purpose library.

As to why cdist is slower than NumPy, I think BLAS is the main reason. The C version implements a naive matrix-vector product.
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/4833a293e7790dd244b2530b74d1a6718cf385d0/scipy/spatial/src/distance_impl.h#L171-L178

That's fine for low dimensional data e.g. for `FEATURES=5` I get SciPy being faster:
```
scipy: 0.02768683433532715
Std: 0.03223299980163574
New: 0.030174732208251953
```

But for 500 dimensions, there's a huge gain from using BLAS. Especially since I think the other versions are all using matrix-matrix BLAS (level 3). 

IMO adding a `gemm`-based version for large dimensional data should make this a lot better.

comments.body:
I happen to come across this issue, and would like to share some idea.

Let $\mathbf X$ be a $p$-by-$n$ matrix with rows denoted by $\mathbf{X}\_i$, $1 \le i \le p$. Similarly, let $\mathbf Y$ be a $q$-by-$n$ matrix with rows denoted by $\mathbf{Y}\_j$, $1 \le j \le q$. Let $\mathbf M$ be an $n$-by-$n$ (inverse covariance) matrix. The goal is to compute matrix $\mathbf D =(d_{ij})$ where $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{M}  (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)’}$. The current C code runs a double loop with a vector-matrix-vector product inside; the time complexity is $O(pqn^2)$ and the space complexity is $O(n)$.

The key to speeding up the calculation is to [whiten](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitening_transformation) the observations first. [Kessy *et al* (2018)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2016.1277159) gave a comparison of several whitening procedures from a statistical perspective. For our purpose, performance is the main concern; and, while the various procedures all have $O(n^3)$ complexity, the constant factor varies by an order of magnitude. The clear winner in terms of speed is Cholesky decomposition.

If $\mathbf M$ is symmetric and nonnegative definite, we could perform Cholesky decomposition and write $\mathbf M = \mathbf L \mathbf L’$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
d_{ij}^2&=(\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{L} ( (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{L})’ \\
&= || (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{L}||^2\\
&=|| (\mathbf X \mathbf L)_i - (\mathbf Y\mathbf L)_j ||^2
\end{align*}
$$

This shows the Malahanobis distance between $\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf Y$ is equal to the Euclidean distance between $\mathbf X\mathbf L$ and $\mathbf Y\mathbf L$, which can be computed quickly. The total time complexity is $O((p+q+n)n^2)$, an order of magnitude lower than the current version. The space complexity is $O((p+q+n)n)$, an order of magnitude higher than the current version.

The code would be something like the following (without error checking etc):

```python
def mahalanobis_via_cholesky(x, y, vi):
    vi = 0.5*(vi+vi.T) # allow psd but non-symmetric matrix; see below
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(vi)
    return cdist(x@L, y@L, 'euclidean')
```

In practice, it might even be advisable that a user perform the transform and then call Euclidean distance directly, because it may as well be the case that the covariance matrix is computed from sample covariance, and the cost of inverting it is equal to the cost of Cholesky decomposition.

If $\mathbf M$ is symmetric but not necessarily positive semidefinite, we could perform SVD and write $\mathbf M = \mathbf U \mathbf \Lambda \mathbf U’$. Then

$$
\begin{align*}
d_{ij}^2&=(\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{U}\mathbf\Lambda ( (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{U})’ \\
&=\mathrm{tr}[ ( (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{U})’ ( (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{U}) \mathbf\Lambda ]\\
&=\mathrm{tr}[ ( (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{U})_i - (\mathbf{Y}\mathbf {U})_j)’ ( (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{U})_i - (\mathbf{Y}\mathbf {U})_j) \mathbf\Lambda ]
\end{align*}
$$

This expression is equal to the squared Euclidean distance between $\mathbf X \mathbf U$ and $\mathbf Y \mathbf U$ with weighted vector $\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Lambda})$, which possibly contains negative entries. The time and space complexity is the same as the Cholesky case.

For general square matrix $\mathbf M$, it may be written as the sum of a symmetric matrix $\mathbf{M}_1$ and an antisymmetric matrix $\mathbf{M}_2$, i.e. $\mathbf M = \mathbf M_1+\mathbf M_2$, where

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbf M_1 &= \frac{1}{2} ( \mathbf M + \mathbf M') \\
\mathbf M_2 &= \frac{1}{2} ( \mathbf M - \mathbf M')
\end{align*}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{align*}
d_{ij}^2 = (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{M}_1  (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)’ + (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)\mathbf{M}_2  (\mathbf{X}_i-\mathbf{Y}_j)’ 
\end{align*}
$$

The first term may be computed using SVD as shown above. And the second term is always zero because the diagonal entries are zero and the off-diagonal entries cancel out. This leads to be following code for general square "inverse covariance" matrix that is possibly indefinite:

```python
def mahalanobis_via_svd(x, y, vi):
    vi = 0.5*(vi+vi.T)
    U, D, _ = np.linalg.svd(vi, hermitian=True)  # vi == U*D*U'
    return cdist(x@U, y@U, 'seuclidean', V=1/D)
```

The speed of the two methods shown above compare favourably with the three solutions in the top post. On my computer, the running time is (lower is better):

```
scipy: 45.31449294090271
Std: 1.8272199630737305
New: 0.13111400604248047
Cholesky: 0.0912330150604248
SVD: 0.22581696510314941
```

One scenario where the proposed methods is expected to be slower than the C implementation is if $p,q \ll n$, such as computing the cdist between two vectors with many elements.

*Remark 1*. The fallback to SVD for indefinite matrix serves to retain backward compatibility. For example, the following code runs fine with the C implementation even though the inverse covariance matrix is indefinite:

```python
cdist([[10,6]], [[5,3]], 'mahalanobis', VI=[[1,0],[0,-1]])
# prints 4.0
```

*Remark 2*. Due to the way the computations are arranged, the C implementation is not guaranteed to 

```python
x = 1.0 + 9*np.finfo(float).eps
y = x / 3
u = np.array([[x,y]])
cdist(2*u, u, 'mahalanobis', VI=[[1,-3],[-3,9]])
# prints nan
```

comments.body:
If the inverse covariance matrix is not given but estimated from the input, then the computations are similar except that a little saving is possible by omitting the inversion and Cholesky decomposition. This seems to have some traction as discussed [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/4815#issuecomment-99231104); see also gh-4815 and gh-4886.

Suppose the covariance is to be estimated from an $m$-by-$n$ matrix $\mathbf Z$ where each row contains one observation. Suppose $m > n$, so that the sample covariance matrix is not singular. Suppose the mean of each column of $\mathbf Z$ is zero; if they are not, they can be centered to be so. The sample covariance matrix is $\mathbf C=\frac{1}{m-1} \mathbf Z’ \mathbf Z$.

To compute $\mathbf C^{-1}$ efficiently, perform QR decomposition of $\mathbf Z$, i.e. write $\mathbf Z=\mathbf Q \mathbf R$ where $\mathbf Q$ is orthonormal and $\mathbf R$ is upper triangular. Then

$$
(m-1)\mathbf C = (\mathbf Q \mathbf R) (\mathbf Q \mathbf R)’=\mathbf R’ \mathbf R
$$

and

$$
\mathbf C^{-1}=(m-1) (\mathbf R’ \mathbf R)^{-1} = (m-1)(\mathbf R^{-1})’ \mathbf R^{-1}
$$

Similar to the reasoning above, the Mahalanobis distance between $\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf Y$ is equal to the Euclidean distance between $\mathbf X (\mathbf R^{-1})’$ and $\mathbf Y (\mathbf R^{-1})’$, times $\sqrt{m-1}$.

The time complexity remains $O((m+p+q)n^2)$, but this method saves unnecessary inversion and SVD (or Cholesky), and guarantees positive definite covariance.

comments.body:
If a nonnegative weight scalar $w$ or vector $\mathbf w$ is supplied, the “weighted” Mahalanobis distance may be defined as

$$
\sqrt{ (\mathbf X_i-\mathbf Y_j) \mathbf W^{\frac 1 2}\mathbf M \mathbf W^{\frac 1 2}(\mathbf X_i-\mathbf Y_j)’}
$$

where $\mathbf W=w \mathbf I$ or $\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf w)$. This is just a matter of left-multiplying $\mathbf L$ or $\mathbf U$ by $\mathbf W^{\frac 1 2}$ and the computations proceed as usual.

I know this is adding not much to what you show here but `vec` x `mat` x `vec` operation in the middle in the current code is significantly slower as @peterbell10 mentioned above. For large arrays this is quite a difference at the sizes you mention that changes your constant in your big O notation.

Grouping this `vec` x (`mat` x `vec`) with a `gemv` and `ddot` calls is going to be your baseline in case you would like to start from an improvement. Then you can decide whether you want to include a `potrf` and a `trtrs` instead of a `gemv` call. Or the `gemm` versions if you want to do it in all one go.

```
from reader_file import FileReader

IDX_FREQ_I = 0
IDX_TIME_J = 1

# Sampling rate, related to the Nyquist conditions, which affects
# the range frequencies we can detect.
DEFAULT_FS = 44100

# Size of the FFT window, affects frequency granularity
DEFAULT_WINDOW_SIZE = 8192 # was 4096

# Ratio by which each sequential window overlaps the last and the
# next window. Higher overlap will allow a higher granularity of offset
# matching, but potentially more fingerprints.
DEFAULT_OVERLAP_RATIO = 0.5

# Degree to which a fingerprint can be paired with its neighbors --

MIN_HASH_TIME_DELTA = 0
MAX_HASH_TIME_DELTA = 200

# not sorting will cut down number of fingerprints, but potentially
# affect performance.
PEAK_SORT = True

# Number of bits to throw away from the front of the SHA1 hash in the
# fingerprint calculation. The more you throw away, the less storage, but
# potentially higher collisions and misclassifications when identifying songs.
FINGERPRINT_REDUCTION = 20

def fingerprint(channel_samples, Fs=DEFAULT_FS,
                wsize=DEFAULT_WINDOW_SIZE,
                wratio=DEFAULT_OVERLAP_RATIO,

    # show spectrogram plot

    print("passed plots")

def generate_hashes(peaks, fan_value=DEFAULT_FAN_VALUE):
    if PEAK_SORT:
      peaks = sorted(peaks, key = lambda x:x[1])

    # bruteforce all peaks
    for i in range(len(peaks)):
      for j in range(1, fan_value):
        if (i + j) < len(peaks):

          # take current & next peak frequency value
          freq1 = peaks[i][IDX_FREQ_I]
          freq2 = peaks[i + j][IDX_FREQ_I]

          # take current & next -peak time offset
          t1 = peaks[i][IDX_TIME_J]
          t2 = peaks[i + j][IDX_TIME_J]

          # get diff of time offsets
          t_delta = t2 - t1

          # check if delta is between min & max
          if t_delta >= MIN_HASH_TIME_DELTA and t_delta <= MAX_HASH_TIME_DELTA:
            h = hashlib.sha1("%s|%s|%s".encode() % (bytearray(freq1), bytearray(freq2),bytearray(t_delta)))
```

There are two issues here; I think they should be treated together.

`gaussian_kde` currently fails with degenerate data of the sort reported above: when the data lies in a subspace (hyperplane) of the space in which it is expressed. ~~[Apparently](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/10205#issuecomment-1111687357), it used to work on this sort of data, so we'd like to get that capability back.~~ It used to be a little more robust to degenerate data because matrix inversion was used instead of Cholesky decomposition. We want to get that level of robustness back.

I think this can be achieved by using `scipy.linalg.ldl` instead of `scipy.linalg.cholesky`. For instance, currently the diagonal of `cholesky`'s `L` matrix is used to get the determinate of the matrix; instead we would use the `D` matrix. Some work is still needed to figure out how to get `whitening` from the LDL decomposition instead of Cholesky. Perhaps that is as simple as using:

comments.body:
@mdhaber I'm using `gaussian_kde` right now and the absence of support for singular matrices is a real pain. I'm willing to do a PR to fix this.

As you wrote above, just using LDL won't really work. The point is that if the matrix is numerically singular in general it is impossible to recover the eigenvalues below the noise level. So a choice has to be made between inflating the below-noise eigenvalues (regularization) and removing them (pseudoinversion).

Inflating means that eigenvalues are set to a minimum value. This can be done with Cholesky by adding a multiple of the identity to the matrix. This "nugget" variance can be chosen with Gershgorin:

```python
def singular_chol(a):
    maxeigv = np.max(np.sum(np.abs(a),axis=1))) # upper bound on the maximum eigenvalue
    eps = maxeigv * len(a) * np.finfo(a.dtype).eps # estimated numerical error floor
    a = a + np.eye(len(a), dtype=a.dtype) * eps # make all eigenvalues at least eps
    return linalg.cholesky(a)
```

If the matrix has been inflated, vectors that have components along the small eigenspaces will produce very low probabilities: `kde.logpdf(x)` will decrease very quickly as `x` deviates from the subspace of the data. Also, the logdet will get a lot of log(eps) terms, so the value of the pdf is heavily influenced by the choice of regularization.

Instead, removing eigenspaces means computing a pseudoinverse. This can be done accurately with a diagonalization, although it could be possible to compute an approximate version with a correction to the Cholesky factor (diagonalization costs 30 choleskies computationally.)

With a pseudoinverse, vectors that have components along the removed eigenspaces are projected orthogonally into the allowed subspace: `kde.logpdf(x)` will give a large value even if `x` is totally implausible. The logdet changes abruptly from one dataset to another as eigenvalues cross the threshold for inclusion.

So there is a substantial behavioral choice between regularization and pseudoinversion.

I'd suggest using regularization, for these reasons:

* From the point of view of the user, it would be unexpected that implausible vectors get a large probability
* Pseudoinversion requires a quite different linalg algorithm
* Pseudoinversion is computationally more expensive

I would do the following:

* ~~remove matrix inversion and use only the Cholesky factor~~ **EDIT** I see it's in 1.10 already
* add the option `allow_singular: bool` to `gaussian_kde.__init__`
* if `allow_singular=False` (default), proceed as usual
* if `allow_singular=True` regularize the matrix before Cholesky. Save the regularization to a public attribute `eps` (which is `None` otherwise)
* document that for numerically singular matrices the probability is not well defined and comparisons between different datasets may be invalid

Decision: should I always regularize if `allow_singular=True`, to lead to predictable behavior, or try first a decomposition without regularization? I think the former is better.

Other decision: should I try again with a larger `eps` if the regularization is not sufficient to get a positive definite matrix? In my experience the regularization I wrote above has always been sufficient, so for starters I'd avoid retries to have a predictable behavior.

Other changes I would do, to `gaussian_kde.resample`:
* support a `np.random.SeedSequence` as `seed` argument
* if there are no weights, assign `_neff` in `gaussian_kde.__init__` to avoid having `neff` different from sample size due to roundoff
* do not use `multivariate_normal`, use directly the cholesky factor of the kde to avoid redundant calculations

Maybe also deprecate `gaussian_kde.inv_cov`?

If I understand correctly, `multivariate_normal` has always taken the "pseudoinverse" approach; the difference is that now there is a "threshold for inclusion" (in your words). Now, after gh-5288, if the argument vector lies outside the threshold to be considered part of the supported subspace, it is assigned a PDF of zero. The threshold is wide enough to accommodate the limitations of floating point arithmetic, but otherwise pretty tight to avoid the user inadvertently experiencing odd behavior near the boundary. This seems like a reasonable compromise for a bug fix (even if we might have made different decisions if we were starting from scratch).

Which methods are you most interested in? My intuition (which may be wrong) is that regularization will make the magnitude of the PDF meaningless, but the ratio between PDFs at different points will be correct. (An example of what I'm thinking: reducing the magnitude used to inflate the eigenvalues will make all the nonzero `lodpdf` values slide upwards together.) Therefore, regularization seems like it could be useful for `resample`, but arguably incorrect (unless the user knows what they're getting into) for `pdf`. With that in mind, I don't think that SciPy's `gaussian_kde` should use regularization for `pdf`/`logpdf`/`evaluate`/`__call__`, but it could be useful to restore the behaviors that used to support singular matrices as mentioned [above](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/10205#issuecomment-1111687357).

comments.body:
I'm interested in both `resample` and `logpdf`.

You are right that the value of the PDF is meaningless in an absolute sense because of the arbitrary regularization. But the same holds for pseudoinversion, since you are arbitrarily removing some directions. Unless the user made sure to always use the same directions, different pdfs would not be comparable as well. Actually, I think that working in a lower-dimensional subspace, and having an abrupt cliff for vectors estimated as out of space, is more surprising than having all very small eigenvalues inflated to a minimum threshold. Moreover, the calculations are not continuous w.r.t. the input matrix, while with regularization they are. Regularization won't break an optimization process, pseudoinversion will.

I think I already took into account all your concerns when I expressed a preference overall for regularization:

> but arguably incorrect (unless the user knows what they're getting into) for pdf

This is why I propose as default `allow_singular=False`, to document the invalidity of absolute comparisons, and to add an attribute for the regularization used.

> but it could be useful to restore the behaviors that used to support singular matrices as mentioned

I've looked at the 1.9 code and it does not really support well singular matrices, it doesn't have clear criteria for the inclusion/exclusion of directions, it is not numerically accurate, and is 5x slower than Cholesky.

I would not switch back to the previous behavior because it is inaccurate and I can't interpret what it is doing. I can't rely on it, I would always have to check manually the covariance matrix to make sure `gaussian_kde` won't mess up.

Doing a proper pseudoinversion would be slow: diagonalization is 30x slower than Cholesky. In general I, and I guess many users, care about speed; if `gaussian_kde` did that, I would write my own implementation with Cholesky.

Overall, this means that I prefer opt-in regularization as a small incremental modification to the current behavior.

If I had to redesign it from scratch, I would use `scipy.stats.Covariance`. But I would like to get a `gaussian_kde` that is able to deal with singular matrices in a well-specified way without slowing it down, and with a reasonable amount of work. I expect that integrating `stats.Covariance` would require some important design changes because its interface is not designed to deal with a function that expects samples as input, and I won't use `gaussian_kde` if it does pseudoinversion.

comments.author: josef-pkt

comments.body:
A thorough discussion. I'll try to reply to everyone.

@josef-pkt 

> speed of computing inverse covariance will be small relative to evaluating the kde on a sample, I guess.

Depends on the number of samples. I'm currently using high-dimension, few samples.

> In general I prefer pinv as default to Ridge because it leaves the results unchanged for the standard non-singular case, while a Ridge penalty always regularizes directions with larger eigenvalues.

(I guess you mean *smaller* eigenvalues) I would like to leave the default behavior unchanged, and add ridge with an option.

> I would make the option nonbinary allowing ridge as alternative, nondefault method.

The point is avoiding adding a lot of stuff to `gaussian_kde` because that should probably be handled together with `stats.Covariance` is some smarter way to be thought about, because there are so many possible options once one starts considering this problem (LOBPCG, Lanczos, LDL, partial Cholesky, corrected Cholesky, series pseudoinversion, who knows what else I'm not even an expert). opt-in ridge currently requires minimal changes.

> If Ridge is only applied after checking for near-singularity, then it looses any or most of the computational advantage to just using always some form of pinv, I guess.

No, trying to do Cholesky and seeing it fail is much faster than doing diagonalization. If you really wanted to look directly at the largest and smallest eigenvalues, you could use LOBPCG, for somewhat large matrices it is faster even though the matrix is dense because it scales like $O(n^2)$.

@ilayn 

> And if this is only for the logdet step then the simplest is to pick eigh (with evr, eigvals_only=True) and threshold the small eigenvalues with max(eigs)*max(m, n)*eps. Still not super nice but at least it moves the noise floor according to the condition number. Cholesky is (or should be) much faster than eigh but I don't know if you would care. Plus you won't be generating the factor itself so saves some memory overhead.

If you want to threshold the small eigenvalues directly, then you are using the full decomposition, so you need to store the factor in memory. Instead, if you only use `eigvalsh` to estimate the higher eigenvalue to implement ridge, you are doing a lot of computations for something that can be estimated quite well with Gershgorin's theorem (`max(sum(abs(x),axis=0)))`). I care about speed in general, Cholesky is 30-40x faster than `eigh`. On my computer, on 10000x10000 matrices, `eigh` takes 1.5 minutes, cholesky 2 seconds. In any case, an nxn factor of some kind has to be stored, so actually I don't understand the comment about the factor, I may be confused.

> So if there is absolutely 100% definitely a positive semidefinite array is sought after and the input cannot be negative definite, then [scipy.linalg.lapack.dpstrf](https://netlib.org/lapack/explore-html/da/dba/group__double_o_t_h_e_rcomputational_ga31cdc13a7f4ad687f4aefebff870e1cc.html) should be good. It is the complete pivoting version of Cholesky and probably fits the bill here. It factorizes as much as it can and then leaves the remaining problematic block intact and you can do whatever you want with it. You can still do two-passes since this is practically still Cholesky (one regular and one with this). But again, maybe I'm missing the point.

Very cool, I did not know about this function. But: I guess that, being pivoted, this is slower than normal Cholesky. On my computer, LDL is typically 5x slower than Cholesky (LDL is pivoted too). I need to check this function to be sure. But this algorithm would have an opaque an unpredictable behavior, and not be more justified than other choices, I address this kind of concern below in reply to @rkern.

@rkern 

> The only thing I really care about is not applying a ridge penalty when the covariance matrix is already fine.

If the user has not specified to allow singular matrices, yes. If the user has specified some option to deal with singular matrices, I'd actually prefer always applying the same calculation without branches.

Example: suppose that one sample was added, which moves a covariance matrix from "fine" to "bad". If the singular-enabled option was active, and it consisted in "try cholesky without ridge, try again with ridge if it fails," this could change some results abruptly.

More concrete example: consider an optimization that uses a simulation (something like simulated inference from the '90s, or a detector geometry Physics simulation I did once). So I have a deterministic function that maps fixed "source" random samples (drawn once and for all) and parameters to some simulated output. The goal is maximizing some function of this output samples w.r.t. the parameters. It is realistic to imagine some of these parameters would change the distribution of the output samples, making the covariance matrix more or less degenerate. If the target function involves a pdf estimation, done with `gaussian_kde`, it is much more useful to have comparable and continuously varying outputs as the parameters are varied, even if some eigenvalues go below the noise level, than satisfying some criterion for "most accurate possible given the circumstances." Ridge with a simple formula for the regularization has this property. Also consider that any method of dealing with below-noise eigenvalues must make some stuff up, there is no "truly correct" method.

@mdhaber 

> So maybe instead of a boolean allow_singular there should be an option for how to treat singular matrices. The default would be None (old behavior), and the only alternative for now would be "regularization" (or "ridge", if that is the preferred term). I would be comfortable with that.

Yup looks fine. I proposed `allow_singular` because I remember seeing it somewhere in numpy/scipy, but since the behaviors are actually different it makes sense to use a different keyword.

I make a ridge-only counter-proposal: `regularization=None` (default) does not use regularization, fails if Cholesky fails. `regularization='auto'` uses Gershgorin. `regularization=<scalar>` adds the given scalar to the diagonal of the matrix (useful for having pdfs comparable across datasets, if needed). The relevance of this choice would be documented under a `Notes` section.

Open-to-future-alternatives proposal: `singular=None`, `singular="ridge"`, `singular="ridge", eps=<scalar>`, where `eps` could be used in the future as threshold/regularization for other algorithms too.

comments.body:
@Gattocrucco You can't have both speed and accuracy for ill-conditioned problems. That's just not going to happen. Either you decompose with `n**3` with a high scalar in front like 30 or 40 or you go with simpler things but axe your way out like cholesky. There is no in between. Your upper bound is also prone to wonky test data. 

Anyways, if `lower=0` then you get the upper trapezoid as the meaningful data. The bottom right `(n-r) x (n-r)` is identical to input data if `n > r`.

```ascii
     [ __________ ]
     [  \        |]
 X = [    \______|]
     [            ]
     [            ]
     [            ]
```

Insane ASCII skills I know. So in the example above, 

```python
# Rank deficient array then salted for ill-conditioning
zzz = np.random.rand(40,38) + 10*np.eye(40, 38)
Z = zzz @ zzz.T + 1e-12*np.eye(40)
X, piv, r, info = la.lapack.dpstrf(a=Z, tol=1e-6)

# Here is the trapezoid
X[r:, :] = 0.
X[:r, :r] = np.triu(X[:r, :r])
P = np.zeros([40, 40])  # You don't need to create P, you can permute directly but better to show this way
P[piv-1, np.arange(40)] = 1.
Err = (P @ X.T) @ (X @ P.T) - Z  # Permuted and trapezoidal Cholesky factors
Err[np.abs(Err) < 1e-12] = 0  # Some cleanup
print(Err)
```

Look at the bottom right corner of `Err`. Funny numbers; almost as if giving the salt back 😉 Then you do whatever you want with the remaning block

According to my wife, they are not the exactly the same outside least squares

system of equations: A x = y

comments.body:
@ilayn 
I wanted to move the discussion from a numerical math view to "statistics".
It's not just system identification or numerically solving an ill-posed problem. 
We want to get a "good" estimator that minimizes some evaluation criterion, eg. mean squared error relative to the "true" parameters, if we have repeatedly the same problem with different data.

Non-negligible (large) ridge factor, Bayesian priors, regularization, penalization provides a better estimator with smaller "loss" in accuracy or smaller variance in repeated sampling. 
We want to have some kind of **optimal** regularization and not just minimally identified.

(
Most work in (frequentist) theoretical statistics and econometrics is in deriving the sampling properties of an estimator. Bayesians and machine learning guys can ignore it because they don't care. Bayes' law for the former and cross-validation for the latter solves all problems in the world. :)
In statsmodels it would sometimes be easy to compute a new estimator, but we don't have inference for it, standard errors and hypothesis test for estimated parameter or predictions. The estimation is relatively easy, the sampling properties are much too difficult. Easy to compute is very often because scipy has the needed tools for the numerical math.
)

comments.body: The nice thing about the multiple of the identity is that it increases all eigenvalues by the same amount, even if you can't look at the individual eigenvalues. This makes it interpretable even though it is computationally simple. This allows you to understand cross-comparisons if you regularize different matrices with the same multiple of the identity.

I re-ran the original reproducer on a current environment and can still reproduce the seed-sensitive behavior, although the failure mode is now cleaner than the old traceback.

Environment:

```text
Python 3.12.13
SciPy 1.18.1
NumPy 2.5.2
```

Using the issue's original covariance matrix and trying seeds `0..19`, some seeds succeed and some raise:

```text
LinAlgError: The data appears to lie in a lower-dimensional subspace of the space in which it is expressed. This has resulted in a singular data covariance matrix, which cannot be treated using the algorithms implemented in `gaussian_kde`. Consider performing principal component analysis / dimensionality reduction and using `gaussian_kde` with the transformed data.
```

I also checked an exactly rank-deficient toy dataset, and it raises the same explicit error. So the old `cholesky(self.inv_cov)` path is no longer the immediate failure point; current `_compute_covariance` caches a Cholesky factor of the data covariance directly.

This suggests that a useful small next step may be a focused reproducer/benchmark that separates:

1. full-rank data where current behavior should stay unchanged,
2. exactly lower-dimensional data where the current explicit error may be correct unless a new API is accepted,
3. near-degenerate data where numerical rank decisions are seed/tolerance sensitive.

I am happy to help turn that into a minimal test/benchmark or draft PR if maintainers think that would move this issue forward. I would avoid proposing diagonal jitter as a default behavior unless there is agreement on the statistical semantics; the existing discussion here makes that boundary pretty clear.

Thanks for the report @edcarter. I can confirm the following still crashes on master:
```
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage.morphology import binary_dilation
from skimage.morphology import disk
inds = np.array(np.random.rand(45, 25) > 0.2)
sm = 32; struct = disk(sm, dtype=bool)
zvals2 = ~binary_dilation(inds,struct, iterations=2)
```

comments.body:
So I've been trying to pinpoint this problem for a while.  Unfortunately, I ran
out of time allocated for this and cannot continue investigating.

However, I have a WIP branch here that detects the out of bounds in the repro
and passes all the tests:

https://github.com/nkaretnikov/scipy/commits/wip-check-buffer-sizes3

I rewrote some macros as functions and added buffer/pointer size checks wherever
I could.  The latter required extending some functions to return buffer sizes.

That said, I'm against merging the above even after a potential clean up.
There's just too many changes for such a widely used project like SciPy.  I
don't want us to break anything by accident.  It would be better to understand
the bug and fix just the bug itself.  Having all those checks in numeric code
that might be called quite a bit seems like a bad idea, for perf reasons, but
also just for readability.  We might also reject potentially valid inputs just
by making a mistake in the checking logic, due to insufficient testing.

About the bug:

The bug triggers in `CASE_ERODE_POINT2` (all names are from my branch) in
`NI_BinaryErosion2`.

Specifically, this needs to be looked at.  The returned value `_to` is added to
an index pointing somewhere in the input array (not always the start of the
array).  After adding `_to` to it, it goes past the memory allocated for the
input array.

```c
npy_intp _to = _offsets[_oo + _hh];
...
if(*(_type *)(_pi + _to) == (_type)_true) {
```

(You can inline the macro to check.)

The functions that influence this are these, especially the last one where
`offsets` is initialized:

```
NI_IteratorGoto
NI_FilterGoto
NI_InitFilterOffsets
```

I ran out of time before I could fully understand the `offsets` layout.  It
generates an array of size:

```
struct dims * struct footprint (set elements) * array elem size
```

E.g., for a 3x3 cross struct:

```
0 1 0
1 1 1
0 1 0
```

This would be:

```
3 * 3 * 5 * sizeof(npy_intp)
```

And then it stores offsets there, which is then indexed in `NI_FilterGoto`
based on the filter (struct) array strides and input array coordinates:

```
*ptrf += itf->strides[ii] * jj;
```

I suspect this relationship between the struct, offsets, and the input array
might be the problem.  Bounds checks in the if-then-else there look suspicious
too, but seem to work(?).

`ptrf` here is `_oo` in `_offsets` above.

IIUC, `NI_BinaryErosion2` is an optimization where the code keeps track of the
regions in the output that have `True` values, which are returned by
`NI_BinaryErosion` (the first call, with `iterations=1`).  I think the idea here
is to only consider the coordinates that can affect the end result without
iterating thru the entire input array.

So, I guess, a potential workaround could be just calling `NI_BinaryErosion`
multiple times, making sure that input/output arrays don't modify each other in
the process, but it would impact performance.  I've tried doing it where
`_nd_image.binary_erosion2` is called but it broke some tests, so perhaps it
needs to be done even earlier.  Maybe I made a mistake somewhere else.  I tried
exploring this for a bit and then ran out of time.

The repro seems to trigger an edge case somewhere in the `offsets` calculation,
I assume.  And it looks like the bug triggers only when the structure's
dimensions are larger than the input and the data has a certain pattern (since
there's a check on the Python side that looks at whether the center of the
struct is 0 or 1 (`cit = _center_is_true(structure, origin)`), but there might
be more code affected by this in the C functions I mention).  For instance, it
doesn't trigger with all zeros and ones, so the placement of boolean values is
important.  There might be also some assumptions about the struct layout, e.g.,
I wonder if the code expects the struct to be similar to the ones generated by
`generate_binary_structure`.

I also wonder if an easy fix would be just disallowing structs with larger dims
than input.  All the examples showcasing binary morphology that I've seen use a
struct smaller than the input, so I'm not sure whether it's even used by anyone
in practice (in the repro above, the struct array is larger because the
parameter to disk is the radius).  But I might be wrong since I'm not working
with morphology code myself.  The original code attempts to support this, I
think.  There are checks comparing input array shape and struct shape.  But as
shown above, it doesn't always work.  Now that I wrote this, I wonder if we even
have struct > input anywhere in the testsuite besides the repro.  Perhaps that's
the bug?  Maybe the checks that I'm referring to above are just to calculate the
difference somewhere (e.g., when the struct partially overlays the input and
goes OOB?) but the code always assumes that the input is larger(?).

For anyone interested in looking at this, I recommend starting by tracing the
code using this test case, which doesn't crash: `test_binary_erosion27` (erosion
and dilation are implemented by the same code).  It uses multiple iterations and
is relatively easy to understand because the inputs are small: you can validate
that the operation works correctly on a sheet of paper too.  Then you can move
on to the repros above.
